statement: In people who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy, evidence is insufficient to say whether harm reduction habits lower the chance of a difficult experience. The one survey read here that measured both (Palmer and Maynard, 2022; pre-registered) asked 163 self-selected, mostly male, experienced people (median 11.5 lifetime uses), reached through university societies and online psychedelic communities, to recall their first experience (a median of 42 months earlier) and their most recent one (a median of 2 months earlier): which listed practices they had used before, during and after, how challenging it had been (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) and how much emotional breakthrough it brought (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory). A score adding up the practices each person used, each weighted by how important the sample rated it for safety, correlated weakly with lower challenge for the first experience (r = −0.21, 95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) and not significantly for the most recent (r = −0.15, −0.30 to 0.00), and with more breakthrough on both occasions (r = 0.24, 0.09 to 0.38), 2 to 6% of the variation (editors' intervals and calculation). The score counted practices after the experience, which cannot have shaped it, was weighted by the respondents' own judgments, was recalled at the same sitting as the outcomes and was not adjusted for anything, and people who stopped after a difficult first experience could not take part. Scores were higher for the most recent experience (48.7 against 40.1), for practices before and after use but not during it, while challenge scores were about the same (17.1 and 17.3% of the maximum). Most were with trusted friends, a practice the sample rated important; few had a sober sitter, which it rated low; and few tested their drugs, although testing was rated important. In a US online panel, 182 of 613 people (29.7%) linked their most challenging experience to having had no preparation; that link went with slightly higher challenge ratings for the same experience, rated at the same sitting (standardized beta 0.09), but not with later thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others (adjusted odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.45) (Simonsson et al., 2023). A mini review that relies heavily on the first survey for its outcome evidence summarizes it as more strategies going with fewer challenging experiences, which overstates it (the score was weighted, and the link with challenge held for the first experience only); the review adds a catalogue of strategies named in the literature and finds outcome research scarce: besides that survey, one preparedness-scale study of psychedelic use (drug class not stated), one ketamine study (design not stated) and, for MDMA, a rapid scoping review whose reference is a preprint, all second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small survey, people who recalled using more safety habits had slightly easier first trips, but not clearly easier recent ones, and the habits counted included things done after the trip. People remembered everything at once, often years later, and those who stopped after a difficult first trip could not take part. A review found almost no other studies of whether these habits work.
population: People who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy: a self-selected survey of experienced people (163) and a US online panel (613); a mini review of the literature
exposure: Harm reduction practices before, during and after use, recalled and weighted by importance; having had no preparation, as a respondent's own explanation of their most challenging experience
comparator: People who recalled fewer or less highly rated practices; respondents who did not link their most challenging experience to having had no preparation
outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), emotional breakthrough (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory), thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others
magnitude: Palmer and Maynard (2022), n = 163: importance-weighted practice score and challenge r = −0.21 (95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) for the first experience, −0.15 (−0.30 to 0.00) for the most recent; with breakthrough r = 0.24 (0.09 to 0.38) on both (editors' intervals; 2% to 6% of the variation). Score 40.06 first against 48.68 most recent; challenge 17.14 against 17.29 per cent of the maximum. Simonsson et al. (2023): no preparation linked to the most challenging experience by 182 of 613; challenge standardized beta 0.09; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others adjusted OR 1.17 (0.56 to 2.45).

risk_of_bias.note: Recalled practices (first experiences a median of three and a half years earlier) weighted by the respondents' own importance ratings and including practices after the experience, outcomes rated at the same sitting, no adjustment, survivor bias (card sc_palmer_2022, overall very high); the panel survey's item is a retrospective attribution, ticked at the same sitting as the challenge rating (sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: The first-experience correlation and the attribution point the same way; the non-significant most-recent correlation is stated.

imprecision.note: Intervals given; the claim is worded as insufficient evidence.

grade.reasoning: Cross-sectional self-report starts low; down two for risk of bias, giving very low. Status single study: the habits-experience association rests on one survey; the panel survey's item is a different measure (an attribution of the worst experience), and the review adds no primary data and misreports the survey, so it is cited only for what it adds. Section 7 (decision p-before-during-after): findings only, for the senior author's approval.
